name: Josephus
label: Outside witness
knownFor: A Jewish priest and historian at Rome, whose Antiquities of the Jews names Jesus and his brother James.
dates: Born in the first year of the emperor Caius, the year 37, by his own Life; he finished the Antiquities in the thirteenth year of Domitian and the fifty-sixth of his life, which William Whiston's note makes the year 93. A note in E. C. Richardson's translation of Jerome says he died after 97

remembered: Origen of Alexandria cites Josephus on John the Baptist and on James against Celsus, and says Josephus "did not accept Jesus as Christ".

Eusebius of Caesarea quotes the longer passage on Jesus in his Church History, and argues that a Hebrew historian's record convicts those who forged acts against Jesus. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, says he is the first writer known to quote it.
Jerome gives Josephus a chapter in his Lives of Illustrious Men, among the church's writers, and copies the passage there with Jesus "believed to be Christ", in E. C. Richardson's English.

uncertain: Which words are his. Our copies of the longer passage say "He was the Christ." Origen, who knew the Antiquities, says Josephus did not accept Jesus as Christ, and Jerome's version says only that Jesus was believed to be Christ. So at least that line was not read as our copies give it. No ancient source used here says how the passage came to read as it does.

How much of the longer passage Josephus wrote was argued four ways in Arthur McGiffert's day, in 1890. Some held it wholly genuine, which McGiffert called "absolutely untenable". Hase, Keim and Schürer held it wholly added, and McGiffert agreed. Gieseler, Weizsäcker, Renan, Edersheim and Schaff held it partly genuine. Ewald held that a hostile Jewish passage was rewritten as praise. McGiffert rejects the suggestion that Eusebius himself put it into the text.

William Whiston, who translated Josephus in the eighteenth century, defended the passage as genuine, while admitting it had "of late been greatly questioned by many". He answers Origen that Josephus did not mean the words as Jews and Christians do, and he held that Josephus was in his own mind a Nazarene or Ebionite Jewish Christian.

The line on Jerusalem's fall. Origen says Josephus blamed the city's fall on the killing of James the Just, and Eusebius and Jerome repeat it. McGiffert says the passage is not found in our existing manuscripts of Josephus, and thinks the copies Origen and Eusebius used held an added line that ours lack.

The phrase naming James as the brother of Jesus. McGiffert notes that some critics doubted it; Neander held it genuine, which McGiffert calls the common opinion of critics, and McGiffert himself sees no good reason to doubt it.

Whiston prints "He was [the] Christ", with the article in brackets as if he had added it. A Greek quotation of the passage, in a martyr-act printed in the Acta Sanctorum for May, has the article. That copy is a later quotation, not Josephus's own text.
Origen's Greek says "our Jesus": he writes as a Christian about a Jewish writer. The printed English, and the brief, leave out the "our".
The year 93 is Whiston's reckoning from Josephus's own dating by Domitian's reign; Jerome says the Antiquities run to the fourteenth year of Domitian.
Josephus's prediction that Vespasian would rule is told by Josephus himself in the Jewish War, where it takes in Vespasian's son as well, and by the Roman writer Suetonius.

Origen of Alexandria, Commentary on Matthew X.17, tr. John Patrick, and Against Celsus I.47, tr. F. Crombie: Josephus was no believer in Jesus as the Christ.
Josephus, Jewish War II.20.4 and Life 65, tr. Whiston: governor of Galilee when the war began, appointed from Jerusalem; in Roman hands before Jerusalem was besieged.
Josephus, Life 76, tr. Whiston: at Rome, an apartment in Vespasian's own former house, Roman citizenship and a pension.
Josephus, Antiquities XX.9.1, tr. Whiston: Ananus brings James, the brother of Jesus called Christ, and some others before the judges and has them stoned.

Origen, Against Celsus I.47, tr. Crombie, and Commentary on Matthew X.17, tr. Patrick: Josephus cited against Celsus; in Origen's Josephus, Jerusalem fell as punishment for the death of James the Just.
Josephus, Antiquities XVIII.3.3, tr. Whiston: the longer passage, the wise man, "He was [the] Christ", condemned to the cross by Pilate, alive again the third day.
Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History I.11.7-9, tr. Arthur McGiffert: the passage quoted as we have it, and the argument against those who forged acts against Jesus.
